1. Global Fuel Price Overview

This analysis covers 84 countries across 7 regions, with 27,468 weekly observations spanning January 2020 to April 2026. The dataset encompasses the COVID-19 demand collapse, the 2022 energy crisis, and subsequent market normalization. Countries are classified across four subsidy tiers (Very High, High, Medium, Low) and three income levels (High, Middle, Low).

2.2 Brent Crude – Retail Price Correlation

At the aggregate level, the Pearson correlation between weekly Brent Crude and the global average retail petrol price is r = 1.0000 (p < 0.001) — a near-perfect relationship because the global average smooths out country-level variation. The policy-relevant metric is the country-level correlation, which has a median of r = 0.999 and ranges from 0.081 to 1.000. This wide range reflects heterogeneity in subsidy regimes, tax adjustments, and market structures that mediate crude-to-pump passthrough.

2.3 Crisis Period Analysis

COVID-19 demand shock (Mar–Jun 2020): Global average petrol fell to $1.202/L, a 17.5% decline from the pre-pandemic average of $1.456/L. Brent Crude hit a low of $47.97/bbl.

2022 energy crisis (Jan–Dec 2022): Average petrol surged to $2.505/L, 9.8% above the full-period average of $2.282/L. Brent Crude peaked at $130.00/bbl. Year 2026 recorded the highest retail price volatility (σ = $1.702/L for petrol).

Key takeaway: The Brent-to-retail passthrough is strong at the aggregate level but highly variable across countries. Country-level correlations range from 0.081 to 1.000, with the subsidy regime being the primary differentiator.

3. Regional Price Disparities

Average petrol prices range from $1.23/L in Middle East to $3.70/L in Europe, a gap of $2.48/L over the full period. This spread reflects differences in taxation, subsidies, refining capacity, and distribution costs.

4. Impact of Subsidies & Taxation on Retail Prices

4.1 Subsidy Level & Retail Prices

The dataset classifies countries into four subsidy tiers. The price gradient across tiers is steep: Very High-subsidy countries average $0.148/L for petrol, while Low-subsidy countries average $3.451/L — a 95.7% price dampening effect. Grouping Very High + High against Medium + Low, the dampening effect is 84.5%.

4.2 Subsidy × Income Level Interaction

The effect of subsidies varies by national income. In high-income countries, the price gap across subsidy tiers is modest; in low-income countries, the gap is far more pronounced, reflecting that subsidies are often the primary mechanism for price control in poorer nations.

Figure 4.3 — Average petrol price by subsidy level, segmented by income classification

4.3 Price Pass-Through from Crude to Retail

The average country-level Brent-to-petrol correlation is r = 0.690 for Very High-subsidy countries versus r = 0.999 for Low-subsidy countries. A lower correlation in high-subsidy countries indicates that government interventions partially decouple domestic prices from international crude movements, buffering consumers but creating fiscal exposure for the state.

Policy insight: Very High-subsidy countries reduce average retail prices by 95.7% compared to Low-subsidy countries, but the trade-off is a fiscal burden that escalates during crude price spikes. The average pass-through correlation is 0.309 lower in Very High vs. Low-subsidy countries, confirming that subsidies dampen — but do not eliminate — crude price transmission.

4.4 Taxation by Subsidy & Income Level

Higher-subsidy countries have lower average tax components, and vice versa. Tax and subsidy policy are complementary levers: countries that subsidize fuel tend to impose lower tax rates, while high-tax countries tend to let market prices prevail.

Figure 4.4 — Left: Average tax percentage by subsidy level. Right: Average tax percentage by income level.

High-income countries impose significantly higher tax rates (avg 34.7%) compared to low-income countries (avg 22.9%), yet their higher purchasing power means the effective burden is lower. Price volatility (coefficient of variation) is higher in low-income countries (64.4%) than high-income countries (42.4%), suggesting that poorer nations are more exposed to crude price shocks despite lower nominal prices.

Energy equity gap: Low-income countries face a double disadvantage — lower nominal prices mask higher relative affordability burdens, and weaker fiscal capacity limits the sustainability of subsidy programs during price spikes.

6. Key Findings & Policy Implications

1
Brent Crude drives retail prices, but passthrough is highly variable across countries.

The median country-level Brent-to-petrol correlation is r = 0.999, but the range spans 0.081 to 1.000. Policymakers should not assume that falling crude prices automatically translate to lower pump prices — local fiscal adjustments and contractual structures create significant lags and asymmetries.

2
2026 was the peak volatility year, with petrol σ = $1.702/L.

The 2022 energy crisis generated the widest price swings. Countries with pre-existing price stabilization mechanisms (automatic tax adjustments, strategic reserves) weathered the shock better. Building institutional capacity for rapid fiscal response is a higher priority than maintaining static subsidy levels.

3
Very High subsidies reduce retail prices by 95.7% vs. Low-subsidy countries, but decouple only partially from crude.

Very High-subsidy countries show a Brent-to-retail correlation of r = 0.690 vs. r = 0.999 for Low-subsidy countries. Subsidies dampen but do not eliminate passthrough. During the 2022 crisis, even Very High-subsidy countries saw significant retail price increases, creating large fiscal outlays. Recommendation: Design subsidies with built-in fiscal caps and automatic sunset clauses triggered when Brent exceeds defined thresholds.

4
Europe pays the most ($3.70/L avg); Middle East pays the least ($1.23/L avg).

The $2.48/L inter-regional spread is driven primarily by tax differentials and subsidy structures, not by supply costs. Recommendation: Tax calibration should consider both revenue needs and competitive positioning — excessively high taxes can incentivize cross-border fuel arbitrage and informal markets.

5
Tax burdens diverge sharply: 34.7% in high-income vs. 22.9% in low-income countries.

This 11.9 percentage-point gap reflects structural differences in fiscal capacity and policy priorities. Recommendation: Low-income countries seeking to increase fuel tax revenue should implement gradual, predictable adjustments paired with targeted cash transfers to protect vulnerable populations — avoiding sudden tax increases that can trigger social unrest.

6
COVID-19 reduced global petrol prices by 17.5%, but the recovery was asymmetric across subsidy regimes.

Prices in Low-subsidy countries snapped back faster than in High-subsidy countries, where governments used the price decline as an opportunity to reduce subsidy outlays rather than pass through the full savings to consumers. Recommendation: Implement transparent, rule-based pricing formulas that ensure symmetry in both upward and downward price adjustments.

7
Price stability is weaker in low-income countries (CV: 64.4%) vs. high-income (CV: 42.4%).

Lower-income economies face greater exposure to international price shocks due to limited hedging instruments and fiscal buffers. Recommendation: Establish regional fuel price stabilization funds that pool risk across multiple low-income countries, enabling counter-cyclical support during price spikes without unsustainable individual fiscal commitments.

Methodology & Data Notes

Analysis is based on 27,468 weekly observations from 84 countries (January 2020 – April 2026). All prices are normalized to USD using historical spot exchange rates. Brent Crude is a global benchmark and is constant across countries within a given week. Tax percentages are estimates and exhibit within-country variability that may reflect methodological or compositional changes. Subsidy classifications comprise four levels: Very High, High, Medium, and Low. Income classifications are High, Middle, and Low. Correlations use the Pearson method. Price volatility is measured as the standard deviation of weekly prices; the coefficient of variation (CV) normalizes this by the mean for cross-group comparison. The Brent-to-retail correlation KPI uses the median of country-level correlations rather than the aggregate-level correlation, as this better reflects the typical country experience. No imputation was applied — all statistics are computed on observed values only.
